account:
Today I have kept my office, mill inspection, lunch, and council-letter appointments. The mill had 76 hay bales available, and the secretary says there are no new council letters. The concrete town proposal I know of is freight's request for lights at both ferry landings and safe marked waiting areas; I have asked the secretary to obtain a cost estimate before approval. I am due at the neighbour's dockside cottage for tea at fifteen, back in the office at sixteen thirty, and at the great hall at eighteen.

Something unusual does seem to be being arranged among the local tradespeople. Reports have linked the baker, builder, innkeeper, and apparently freight to discussions at the bakery, sometimes described by villagers as involving bridge or port changes. I have not confirmed any such change. Yesterday I saw the builder give the baker planks and a lantern. Today the innkeeper said an outstanding bread delivery had arrived and no extra order was necessary. Those supplies could be ordinary business or connected with preparations; I cannot tell from what I have seen.

The strongest explanation is the civic presentation booked for eighteen to eighteen thirty. The secretary's written supplement explicitly describes appreciation of municipal public service from the inn and local tradespeople. It says the organisers need time to prepare around their work and that I should arrive at eighteen, not earlier. The innkeeper will meet me outside shortly beforehand and escort me in. Their insistence on the exact time, combined with supplies and bakery conversations, makes me suspect a coordinated appreciation gathering, perhaps with refreshments and decorations, whose details they want to keep from me until then. That is an inference, not something I have witnessed. The neighbour's tea invitation may simply be our regular appointment; I have no evidence that it is part of the preparations.
